senses: A small salmon with red flesh, Oncorhynchus nerka, found in the coastal waters of the northern Pacific.
Edible flesh of this fish.
ety: Borrowed from Halkomelem sθəqəy̓, probably meaning red fish.

senses: The urge of a person to work excessively; ergomania.
A sharp tower of ice formed by intersecting crevasses of a glacier.
ety: From Swiss French sérac (“kind of cheese; sharp tower of ice”), from Franco-Provençal sera, seré, from Latin seraceum, from serum (“whey”), from Proto-Indo-European *ser- (“to flow, run”). Sense 2 is from the resemblance of the towers of ice to the cheese, which tends to cleave into rectangular pieces.

senses: one who owns a concession or a franchise
β-phenyl-GABA, a gabapentinoid drug similar to baclofen and gabapentin, often legally sold online and taken orally for its euphoric effects.
A traditional Japanese wood- or charcoal-fired earthen vessel used as a stove or oven.
A modern cooker in this style, often used for barbecues.
An Irish music festival with competitions for the best performance on various instruments.
ety: From Irish fleadh, classical/dialectal/superseded spelling of fleá, from Old Irish fled, from Proto-Celtic *wlidā.

senses: A clerk; a scrivener.
ety: Borrowed from Spanish escribano. Doublet of scrivener and scrivano.

senses: A very fine starch powder derived from corn (maize) used in cooking as a thickener, to keep things from sticking, or as an anti-caking agent.
Being uniformly sensitive across the entire visible range, and thus reproducing colours faithfully
Sensitive to all colours except red
A tool used to pare things.
A pencil sharpener.
examples: A: 'yea like I used to have all these little parers and little fancy girly parers but then I was like I'd probably get into trouble ... people would be like 'why do you have that'... so I went for a plain pencil parer'.

senses: Any of several similar plants within the subfamily Faboideae.
ety: From Middle English vecche, fecche, ficche, from Old Northern French veche, variant of Old French vece, from Latin vicia. Doublet of fitch.

senses: One who idles; one who spends their time in inaction.
One who idles; a lazy person; a sluggard.
A mechanical device such as a pulley or wheel that does not transmit power through its own axle, but forms part of a gear train, supports a moving belt, etc.
A metasediment.
examples: The absence of sedimentaries and metasedimentaries in W52 suggest it is not from the Sepik north coast, which is defined by heterogeneous lithic inclusions derived from the Torricelli Mountains.

senses: A system administrator; a person whose job it is to maintain computer or network systems.
examples: Many front-end web developers may not have implemented a web service before, leaving that boring stuff to the neckbeards and the sysadmins.

senses: That which catalyzes.
A catalytic converter.
The Orange Revolution protests that took place in Kiev’s Maidan in 2004–05; the Euromaidan protests of 2013–14; the protest movement associated with the 2014 Ukrainian Revolution.
ety: From Майда́н Незале́жності (Majdán Nezaléžnosti, “Independence Square”) in Kiev, from Ukrainian майда́н (majdán, “square”), from Ottoman Turkish میدان (meydan), from the same Persian source as above.

senses: The amount that will fit into a basket
ety: From Middle English basket ful, baskett full, equivalent to basket + -ful.

senses: A pale, dry fino sherry.
A kind of small roundish olive with a small freestone pit, a fine skin, and a somewhat bitter taste.
ety: Probably named for the town near Seville.
examples: Manzanillas are commonly pitted and stuffed with Spanish pimientos.

senses: Having the character of an epiphany.
examples: And he knows the value of an epiphanic feed.

senses: Steller's sea cow, an extinct sirenian.
ety: After Georg Wilhelm Steller, German naturalist.

senses: One who makes a covenant.
To replace stale or noxious air with fresh.
To circulate air through a building, etc.
To provide with a vent.
To expose something to the circulation of fresh air.
To expose something to public examination or discussion.
ety: From Middle English, borrowed from Latin ventilātus, past participle of ventilō.

senses: Containing dissolved salts of iron.
Tasting of iron.
ety: From Ancient Greek χάλυψ (khálups, “steel”) + English -ate (adjective-forming suffix).

senses: A person who trains another; a coach, a trainer.
ety: Borrowed from Cebuano trainor, itself from English trainer.

senses: Synonym of deltaic.
A system of government by a president.
examples: Presidentialism is the dominant form of government in the continental Americas.

senses: A small design etched on the margin of a plate and supposed to be removed after the earliest proofs have been taken.
Any feature distinguishing a particular stage of the plate.
A print or proof distinguished by such a mark.
A person who uses a harpoon, especially to hunt whales.
examples: Y.T. laughs. So does Raven. "What's your job?" Y.T. asks. "I'm a harpooner," he says.

senses: A hard yellow deposit on the teeth, formed from dental plaque.
ety: From Old French tartre, from Medieval Latin tartarum, from Byzantine Greek τάρταρον (tártaron), said to be from Arabic دُرْدِيّ (durdiyy), though it is already found in Pelagonius’s Ars veterinaria 46 in the adjective tartarālis, if the reading is correct. Arabic etymon from Persian درد (dord, “dreg”) from Proto-Iranian *dr̥ti- (“manure, feces”), from Proto-Indo-European *dʰṛ-to-, from Proto-Indo-European *dʰreyd- (“to have diarrhea”), whence also doublet of dirt.

senses: Any of five sheaths that are thought to cover the Atman, or True Self, according to Vedantic philosophy.
A particular type of Sanskrit dictionary.
ety: Borrowed from Sanskrit कोश (kóśa, “sheath, vessel, container, layer”).

senses: destruction, apocalypse
A period of cosmic inactivity, lasting 4.32 billion years.
Having been made smooth.
One who, or that which, defuses.
Any piece of equipment used to homogenize mixtures, such as a kitchen blender, mortar and pestle, ultrasonic bath, etc.
A slip, lapse, or error.
ety: Borrowed from Latin lāpsus. Doublet of lapse.

senses: One who picks or forages for berries.
A three-horse chariot used by the Ancient Romans.
ety: From Latin triga, a contraction of ter or tri- (“thrice”) + iuga (“yoked”).

senses: The act of dismantling; disassembly.
Full of light; bright.
ety: From Middle English lightful, lihtful (“luminous, providing enlightenment”), from light, liht (noun) + -ful (“full of (a feeling)”, suffix forming adjectives). See more at light (noun).
